title: A torus and a commuting rational point lie in a common Borel subgroup
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A torus is a group scheme $T$ isomorphic over $k$ to $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected, let $T\subseteq G$ be any torus, and let $c\in G(k)$ satisfy $c_At=tc_A$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and every $t\in T(A)$. A Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup of $G$, with solvable meaning that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. There exists a Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ such that $T\subseteq B$ as subgroup schemes and $c\in B(k)$. No maximality of $T$ is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 17.37 and its proof, printed p.363: the assertion actually proved for each c is existence of a common Borel. The parenthetical finite-union assertion is not included (it fails for the trivial torus).

proof.text: Choose a Borel subgroup $B_0$ by [lem-sfb-borel-conjugation-cover]. By [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] form the separated finite-type quotient $q:G\to X=G/B_0$; it is faithfully flat, and $(g,b)\mapsto(g,gb)$ identifies $G\times B_0$ with $G\times_XG$. The left action is $h\cdot q(g)=q(hg)$: multiplication preserves right cosets after every base change, so it descends through the represented fppf coset sheaf. The unit and associativity identities follow from those of $G$ on local lifts.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, choice of B and the action on G/B; quotient geometry: Theorem 17.9(a), p.354.

proof.text: The map $q$ is of finite presentation and detects cosets. It is locally of finite type by [lemma-nagata-finite-type-to-separated-target](a), and $X$ is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian], so $q$ is locally of finite presentation by [pqf-lem-lft-fp-locnoeth]; as $G$ is affine and $X$ separated, [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence](1) makes $q$ quasi-compact and of finite presentation. On a test scheme $T$ the kernel-pair isomorphism says $q(a)=q(b)$ exactly when $a^{-1}b\in B_0(T)$.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, the quotient G/B and completeness of G/B used there; Theorem 17.9(a), p.354, and the quotient properties of 5.20–5.28, pp.104–105.

proof.text: Points of $X$ lift fpqc locally, and $X$ is proper. For $x\in X(T)$ the projection $T'=G\times_XT\to T$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-base-change, lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change, lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence](3); the preimage of an affine open is quasi-compact, so finitely many affine opens of $T'$ map onto it, and $\{T'\to T\}$ is an fpqc covering [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering] on which $x$ is the image of the first projection. With the preceding step, $q$ is a quotient as required by [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry]; $B_0$ is smooth, connected, closed and maximal among smooth connected solvable subgroups, so that node makes $X$ proper over $k$.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, the quotient G/B and completeness of G/B used there; Theorem 17.9(a), p.354, and the quotient properties of 5.20–5.28, pp.104–105.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-borel-conjugation-cover] to $c$ and $B_0$: choose $g_0\in G(k)$ and $b_0\in B_0(k)$ with $c=g_0b_0g_0^{-1}$. Then $c\cdot q(g_0)=q(g_0b_0)=q(g_0)$. Thus the equalizer of $c:X\to X$ and $\mathrm{id}_X$ has a $k$-point.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, nonemptiness from Theorem 17.33(b), p.362.

proof.text: Define $Y=X\times_{X\times_kX}X$ using $(c\cdot-,\mathrm{id}_X):X\to X\times_kX$ and the diagonal. On every test scheme its points are exactly the $x$ satisfying $c\cdot x=x$. Since $X$ is separated, its diagonal is closed [def-weil-proper-morphism]; [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change] makes $Y\hookrightarrow X$ closed. By [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-proper], $Y$ is proper over $k$, hence of finite type by [def-weil-proper-morphism]. It is nonempty by the preceding step; no reduction or smoothness of $Y$ is required.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, the closed c-fixed subscheme of G/B.

proof.text: The action of $T$ restricts to $Y$. Indeed, on every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, for $t\in T(A)$ and $y\in Y(A)$, the given commutation identity gives $c_A\cdot(t\cdot y)=t\cdot(c_A\cdot y)=t\cdot y$. This holds after arbitrary base change and therefore factors the morphism $T\times Y\to X$ through the defining equalizer $Y$. Unit and associativity restrict from the action on $X$.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, T stabilizes the c-fixed subscheme.

proof.text: Every torus is smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-type-largest-subtorus]. Since $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$, its test-algebra groups are commutative, so its commutator morphism is the unit and it is solvable. Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-proper-fixed-point] to this smooth connected solvable group acting on the nonempty proper finite-type scheme $Y$. Obtain $y\in Y(k)$ fixed by $T$ after every algebra extension. By [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry], its image in $X(k)$ lifts to some $g\in G(k)$.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, second use of the Borel fixed point theorem 17.3; smooth connected tori: Definition 12.14 and paragraph following, p.236.

proof.text: Put $B=gB_0g^{-1}$. Conjugation is a group-scheme automorphism, so $B$ is closed, smooth, connected, solvable and maximal with these properties: a larger such subgroup conjugates back to one larger than $B_0$. For every $k$-algebra $A$ and $t\in T(A)$ we have $q(tg_A)=t\cdot y_A=y_A=q(g_A)$. The kernel-pair identity of [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] gives $g_A^{-1}tg_A\in B_0(A)$; hence $T(A)\subseteq B(A)$ naturally in $A$, which is the subgroup-scheme containment $T\subseteq B$. Likewise $c\cdot y=y$ gives $g^{-1}cg\in B_0(k)$ and $c\in B(k)$.

source.place: Lemma 17.37, p.363, displayed coset equalities and final conjugation.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 17.37, printed p.363, fixed-locus proof; Theorem 17.33(b), p.362, for the first fixed point.
